0.1 Context
This Quarto Manual is the human-facing source of truth for constructing and operating the Madagascar Healthshed Clinic Data pipeline. Its emit profile materializes reviewed configuration and command-line tools. Scientific work is then run explicitly through the generated container runner and targets graph.
In MDG, our research has divvied up the geographical land into “healthsheds.” Healthsheds conceptually represent a catchment area in which nearby residents are expected, under normal circumstances, to attend a central clinic for their healthcare. In doing so, we can ask interesting questions about health as it pertains to an individual’s residential healthshed, and investigate what confounds and other variables influence health outcomes. Importantly, we are also able to use the healthsheds for geospatial data analysis questions, such as by aggregating ERA5 satellite data to each healthshed, and seeing if environmental exposures to heat, precipitation, etc., contribute to health outcomes.

In our reproduction of the pipeline, we expect the same truth to hold in implementation. This manual can be read in several ways.
Each workflow page follows the Quarto Manuals page contract: one prerequisite block establishes the starting state, one or more procedure blocks perform the work, and one check block verifies the outcome. Target declarations, file writes, and execution commands belong in procedures. Checks inspect the resulting targets or artifacts through assertions, summaries, plots, or test commands. Read the prose before each code chunk for its inputs, action, and expected result.
Long transformations are divided into named stages so the operator can inspect their handoffs. Dependencies between pages live in targets and tracked files. The public authoring render executes no protected-data analysis; diagnostic chunks are for an authorized data session, and synthetic tests can run without the staged sources.

title: 2  Data Curation Manual
text:
This manual walks the reader through a declarative reproduction of the MDGHealthshedClinicData Prospector.
Clinic data from Madagsascar is imported from legacy Google Drive uploads. The data spans several years from 2010 to 2024, with prospective data to be added 2025 onwards. GESIS is the prior format, where each row in a GESIS file is a count of GESIS codes and likewise for DHIS2 data. Diagnoses are translated and linked by several crosswalks and manual fixes recorded in the code.
The manual should:

declaratively create a robust, reproducible computational environment;
safely and declaratively stage input data;
process the data transparently and elegantly;
version and distribute the data to the Frontier.

The Manual separates three operations:

an authoring render produces human-readable documentation;
an emission render synchronizes reviewed scripts and configuration;
the emitted container runner executes R and the targets pipeline.

No render is permitted to inspect or transform protected source data.

# Madagascar Healthshed Clinic Data

This repository contains the executable curation Manual for the Madagascar
Healthshed Clinic Data pipeline. The Manual owns generated configuration and
command-line entry points; scientific execution occurs explicitly through a
Singularity container and a targets graph.

## Current status

Infrastructure and an input-inventory target are scaffolded. Source selection,
schema interpretation, pre-/post-DHIS2 reconciliation, missing-value rules,
disclosure controls, and release design remain documented human decisions.

No protected data is rendered into the Manual or committed to this repository.

## Render the Manual

```sh
scripts/render-isolated --profile authoring
scripts/render-isolated --profile emit
```

The authoring profile updates the rendered Manual. The emit profile also
synchronizes generated scripts and configuration from reviewed `.qmd` source.

## Build and operate the environment

Follow the rendered Infrastructure pages in `docs/infrastructure/`. After the
runtime image and frozen R library exist:

```sh
scripts/mdg-healthshed-clinic-data
scripts/mdg-healthshed-clinic-data exec uvr run scripts/run-pipeline.R
```

With no subcommand, the container runner opens a shell in the repository.
Commands require the explicit `exec` subcommand.

3.2 Workflow data storage convention
Across our workflows, keep all data in targets objects or in Parquet files tracked as file targets. In-memory tables, lists, and spatial sf objects remain ordinary targets. When a transformation persists data outside the target store, it writes Parquet and returns the path from a target declared with format = "file". A path stored in an ordinary character target does not itself track the file’s contents. A _parquet suffix documents the format; it does not replace the file-target declaration.
Staged source files retain their original CSV, Excel, ZIP, or spatial formats and provenance, and are also tracked as file targets. Temporary extraction and scratch files can exist within a target’s execution; downstream stages consume the returned object or tracked Parquet artifact. Diagnostic notebook queries use tar_read() or tar_load() and do not create separate persistent data copies. Ordinary targets may use RDS internally in the target store; the convention concerns how workflow data is handed between stages.
In tangled notebooks, #| format: file applies to every assignment in that code chunk. Keep path declarations in separate chunks from in-memory data transformations so tables are not accidentally declared as file paths.

3.4 How the responsibilities connect
Three different kinds of mapping are involved. The facility mapping links a year-specific GESIS code to a DHIS2 facility UID. The clinic identity crosswalk follows a clinic through code and name changes. The diagnosis dictionary defines comparable measurement variables across reporting systems. The first two identify who reported; the third defines what was reported.
The spatial branch assigns administrative areas called fokontany (FKT) to clinics and unions their polygons into healthsheds. These are based on the 2022 sectorization. Their use alongside earlier reporting data does not itself establish historical catchment boundaries.
The diagram shows the intended scientific handoffs, including proposed notebooks. It is a responsibility map, not a claim that all these dependencies are already implemented in _targets.R.











The Wave 3 preparation script also reads the original facility mapping to attach descriptive columns. It does not read the cleaned mapping produced by script 1. That separate use is described below because it affects join cardinality and should remain visible during migration.

text:
3.5 0 — Prepare the Wave 3 source table
Source: 0_prep_w3_kevin_translated.R. Destination: 18_page-prep-w3.qmd.
This script translates the earlier Wave 3 preparation into R. It recursively reads the RMA CSV exports, adjusts inferred logical columns to numeric so that sparsely populated measurements can be read, drops two organisation-unit description/code fields, and combines the tables. It then groups by organisationunitid and periodname, taking the maximum of each remaining field and replacing numeric negative infinity from all-missing groups with missing values. This is a maximum rule, not an addition of reports. See CSV type handling, lines 25–38; file discovery, column removal, and combination, lines 43–81; maximum reduction, lines 161–168.
Next, it reads the original DHIS2–GESIS mapping, selects facility UID, GESIS code, type, and name, removes exact duplicates and missing UIDs, and joins those attributes to the Wave 3 data by UID alone. It adds the legacy V1 row index. Finally, for periods after 202300, it substitutes three renamed breastfeeding and mosquito-net fields into their earlier column names and drops the replacement columns. See crosswalk preparation, lines 191–212; UID join and row index, lines 233–243; period-specific substitutions, lines 264–272.
Handoff: the script writes data/raw/from_Kevin/wave3_with_keys_may2_v3.csv. Scripts 3 and 4A instead read wave3_with_keys.csv. The prepared table supplies both measurements and the column names/order used by the diagnosis dictionary. See script 0 output, lines 274–275; script 3 input and column numbering, lines 31–48; script 4A input, line 249.
Context for notebook 18: explain the two reductions now used to avoid holding all source tables in R: maximum within each file, then maximum across the file summaries. Explain all-missing behavior separately from zero values. The UID-only descriptive join can repeat a row when a UID has several mapping records; grouping the mapping by UID in the legacy script did not make it unique. Record the expected cardinality rather than assuming one UID implies one output row. The script’s opening comment limits scope to 2020–2022, but its reader is recursive and its final substitutions explicitly address 2023; the actual supported input period needs an explicit contract. See stated scope, lines 1–6; recursive reader, lines 51–53; 2023 substitutions, lines 264–272.
The replacement notebook already contains the per-file DuckDB reader and reducer, cross-file reduction, descriptive join, and substitutions. Its stopping-point prose and crosswalk input variable names are not yet consistent with all of that code. Treat it as a migration in progress.

3.6 1 — Clean the DHIS2–GESIS facility mapping
Source: 1_clean_mapping_dhis2_gesis.R. Destination: 19_page-clean-mapping-dhis2-gesis.qmd.
This script prepares the bridge between historical GESIS facility codes and DHIS2 UIDs. It reads the original mapping and gives the four UID columns explicit region, district, commune, and facility names. It removes 2022 and the invalid Belalanda code, applies reviewed GESIS-code corrections, and fills a known missing facility UID. See source mapping and exclusions, lines 11–18; code checks, corrections, and known UID fill, lines 25–58.
The remaining work applies the reviewed workbooks and CSVs: fill other missing UIDs; interpret annotations for UID-years associated with multiple GESIS codes as keep, rename, or delete decisions; add reviewed codes absent from the original mapping; and apply individual corrections discovered while comparing the mapping with diagnosis data. Deletions use the relevant year, code, and UID so that an unrelated record sharing a code is not removed accidentally. See additional UID fills, lines 64–71; annotation interpretation, lines 83–89; keyed deletions and renames, lines 143–163; missing-code additions, lines 175–196; individual corrections, lines 201–231.
Handoff: data/intermediate/mapping_gesis_dhis2_clean.csv. Script 2 uses it to assign clinic identities, and script 5 uses its 2018 records to recover historical sectorization links. The new notebook exposes s1_gesis_xwalk_clean_df for downstream targets. See legacy mapping output, lines 277–278; script 2 mapping use, lines 57–79; script 5 historical mapping use, lines 309–328.
Context for notebook 19: each correction needs its source evidence, join keys, expected effect, and a diagnostic. A GESIS code may legitimately map to different UIDs over time, and a UID-year may retain multiple GESIS codes; a global one-to-one assertion would change the legacy interpretation. The notebook already separates the eight legacy stages and retains multiplicity and name checks. Those checks document exceptions to interpret, not a reason to merge or discard records automatically. See legacy multiplicity and name diagnostics, lines 235–274.

section: 3.7 2 — Construct longitudinal clinic identities for Waves 1–2
text:
3.7 2 — Construct longitudinal clinic identities for Waves 1–2
Source: 2_wave1-2_construct_clinicID.R. Destination: 20_page-construct-clinic-ids.qmd.
The script starts from an inventory of distinct clinic records in each monthly file. The six identifying fields are clinic name, year, month, commune code, facility code, and source-file number (fname). Its active code reads an already saved inventory; the code that originally built that inventory is commented out. See commented inventory construction and active read, lines 22–37.
It corrects facility codes using the reviewed workbook and joins the cleaned mapping by corrected code and mapping year. In 2015, January–March use old GESIS codes and later months use new codes, except that records from fname == 1 retain the old codes. Three explicit exceptions prevent known incorrect UID assignments. Within a corrected-code/name pair, it fills an unambiguous UID, then fills missing type and mapped name from the group’s mode. The mode helper resolves ties by first occurrence, so input order matters. See code corrections, lines 42–50; 2015 mapping and three exceptions, lines 63–79; UID and attribute propagation, lines 98–125; mode tie behavior, lines 7–15.
The initial clinic_ID is the UID when available, otherwise corrected GESIS code plus cleaned clinic name. The script marks reviewed deletions with a missing ID, reconciles identities using verified shortened GESIS codes (“snips”), and then uses commune/name groups to reconcile remaining identities. Four ambiguous snips and the 2014 110543027 exception remain excluded from the relevant reconciliation rules. See provisional identity, lines 143–156; reviewed deletions, lines 158–169; verified snips and exclusions, lines 177–205; commune/name reconciliation and exception, lines 209–221.
Handoff: data/intermediate/w2010_2019_clinicID.rds and .csv, retaining original matching fields, corrected code, mapped type, and ID_checked. That flag records whether any mapped type in the identity group contains CSB; it is not a general certification that the identity is correct. Scripts 4A, 6, and 7 consume this crosswalk. See ID_checked definition and crosswalk outputs, lines 223–233.
Context for notebook 20: distinguish source inventory, code correction, year-aware UID assignment, UID propagation, provisional identity, reviewed deletion, and the two reconciliation steps. The current notebook rebuilds the inventory from the staged ZIP in DuckDB, decoding Windows-1252 before reduction and preserving file/row order. It contains both the newer Parquet correction and mapping targets and the longer R transformation that repeats those operations from the inventory. This duplication is an open refactoring boundary: document which intermediate each later step should consume before removing either route. Compare identities and exception records with the legacy result, including missing IDs and mode ties.

section: 3.8 3 — Construct the diagnosis dictionary across waves
text:
3.8 3 — Construct the diagnosis dictionary across waves
Source: 3_construct_dictionary.R. Replacement: 21_page-construct-diagnosis-dictionary.qmd, existing and in development.
This script defines comparable variables across Wave 1, Wave 2, Wave 3A (2020), and Wave 3B (2021–2022). It combines the earlier-wave dictionary, reviewed cross-wave diagnosis mappings, actual Wave 3 column names, a separate 2020 anemia export, and supplementary diagnoses. It replaces the original Wave 1 diarrhea/pneumonia definitions and adds AVC and ULGEN entries that were absent from the main dictionary. See source dictionaries and replacement diagnoses, lines 31–66; AVC, ULGEN, and diarrhea/pneumonia additions, lines 69–92.
It interprets mapping notation such as alternatives, ranges, and sums; joins source descriptions to column identifiers; and aggregates source variables into common definitions. The within-Wave-3 mapping handles changed age bands and disease definitions, including anemia, severe acute malnutrition, and suspected versus confirmed diabetes. It retains earlier-wave variables without a Wave 3 match, excludes designated ignored categories, and assigns output variable names such as V1, V2, and so on. These V variables identify harmonized measurements; they have a different role from the Wave 3 source table’s V1 row index. See within-Wave-3 definition changes, lines 105–162; common-definition aggregation, lines 178–205; mapping notation and wave joins, lines 208–277; unmatched variables and V identifiers, lines 280–299.
The later stages enrich the dictionary with French and English descriptions, diagnostic-code descriptions, reporting-table descriptions, available waves, and output-file groups. They use existing translated material, live gtranslate calls, and manual wording corrections. The filename column partitions variables into 40 groups for diagnosis output. See existing translations and live diagnostic-code translations, lines 307–357; description assembly, wave availability, and output groups, lines 446–486; reporting-table translations and final wording corrections, lines 514–561.
Handoff: the active final write is scratch/dictionary_test2.csv, while script 4A expects data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv. The missing promotion or rename step is not established by this script. The dictionary’s per-wave expressions and filename assignments drive measurement cleaning. See dictionary scratch output, lines 580–581; script 4A dictionary input, lines 29–31.
Context for the replacement: explain source dictionaries and supplements, cross-wave equivalence rules, expression construction, and descriptive enrichment as separate stages. Wave 3 X1, X2, etc. are assigned from the prepared table’s column order, even though several joins now match on descriptions. Record that schema explicitly so a changed reader or column order cannot silently change a diagnosis. Preserve translation provenance rather than treating a fresh network translation as a fixed input. Checks should establish that referenced columns exist, summed terms are distinct, and each source-expression mapping is used as intended. See positional X identifiers, lines 31–48; mapping uniqueness and repeated-summand checks, lines 563–578.
The replacement notebook now records the prepared Parquet schema in s3_w3_column_dictionary_df, appending only missing anemia column names. It reduces replacement diarrhea/pneumonia inputs to unique definitions in DuckDB before collecting them. s3_diagnosis_dictionary_df is the small in-memory handoff, and s3_diagnosis_dictionary_parquet persists it as a file target. The graph declares these stages; it has not been executed as part of this migration.
Translations reuse the archived original description translations and the bilingual data/clean/diagnosis_dictionary_translated.csv member in the staged ZIP. s3_diagnosis_translation_provenance_df records those source members. Grouped diagnostic-code phrases are matched exactly after assembly; this replaces the legacy live translation calls without splitting phrases on punctuation. Conflicting lookup pairs fail, missing required code/table translations appear in s3_diagnosis_translation_gaps_df and stop the final handoff, and missing general English descriptions remain visible for review. The archived dictionary supplies translations only, not harmonized IDs or mapping expressions.

section: 3.9 4A — Clean measurements and combine reporting waves
text:
3.9 4A — Clean measurements and combine reporting waves
Source: 4A_clean_clinic_diagnosis.R. Proposed destination: 22_page-clean-clinic-diagnosis.qmd.
This is the main measurement transformation. It consumes the clinic-ID crosswalk, diagnosis dictionary, monthly tall Waves 1–2 files, prepared Wave 3 data, and supplementary AVC, diarrhea/pneumonia, and anemia exports. The identity work determines which clinic a report belongs to; the dictionary determines how its measurements become comparable variables. See identity and dictionary dependencies, lines 29–51; earlier-wave source files and supplements, lines 108–128.
For Waves 1–2, it replaces the superseded Wave 1 diarrhea/pneumonia records, adds supplements, normalizes variable names, joins clinic IDs, and excludes the explicitly problematic UID qCHtCHkwqtQ. It drops clinic-month/file groups whose total reported value is not positive. Duplicate handling distinguishes identical repeats, differences caused only by missing values, and distinct values that the legacy rules sum. Unhandled conflicts receive the -99 sentinel. It then pivots measurements wide, adds expected but absent columns, and evaluates the dictionary separately for the two waves. See supplements, identity join, exclusions, and reporting filter, lines 121–154; duplicate classification and reductions, lines 160–196; wide conversion and dictionary evaluation, lines 198–236.
For Wave 3, it inserts the separate 2020 anemia data, assigns the positional X names expected by the dictionary, drops exact duplicate records, converts negative values in three designated variables to missing, and removes rows without positive measurements while excluding refrigerator-temperature fields from that reporting check. It applies Wave 3A expressions to 2020 and Wave 3B expressions to the later periods. See 2020 anemia insertion, lines 271–287; column numbering, deduplication, negatives, and reporting filter, lines 293–324; Wave 3A and 3B evaluation, lines 329–344.
Finally, it combines the waves and resolves overlapping reports using the expected source file for each period. It prefers that file when present; otherwise it keeps the closest available file number. The same selection logic supplies the reporting-history table. See reporting-history selection, lines 350–373; combined outputs and overlapping-file selection, lines 382–418.
Handoff: data/clean/by_diagnosis/<filename>.feather, separate <filename>_wrong_fname.feather files for discarded overlapping reports, and data/clean/by_diagnosis/clinic_reporting_track.feather. The tracking table records which file supplied each clinic-month, using zero for no retained report. Script 7 expects the tracker at data/intermediate/clinic_reporting_track.feather; the source scripts do not establish the intervening move or copy. See script 4A output directory, lines 22–25; tracker values and write, lines 350–373; retained and rejected diagnosis outputs, lines 404–418; script 7 tracker input, line 21.
Context for the replacement: document earlier-wave cleaning, Wave 3 cleaning, dictionary application, report selection, and output partitioning separately. The duplicate rules here differ from the maximum rule in script 0. Missing values, entered zeros, the temporary -1 missing-value sentinel, and the -99 conflict sentinel have different meanings. In sums, earlier-wave -1 values and Wave 3 missing values are replaced with zero; this does not justify replacing every missing measurement with zero. Preserve the excluded UID, negative-value rules, and fname tie behavior as explicit decisions to review during migration. See wave-specific missing values in sums, lines 53–72; temporary -1 sentinel, lines 198–200.

text:
3.11 5 — Reconcile sectorization and construct 2022 healthsheds
Source: 5_clean_sect2022_construct_healthsheds.R. Proposed destination: 23_page-construct-healthsheds.qmd.
This script connects the 2022 sectorization’s FKT assignments to administrative polygons, then unions the assigned polygons for each clinic. Its inputs include the sectorization table, OCHA/BNGRC boundaries and code lookup, reviewed matching files, manual geolocation corrections, the 2018 sectorization, and the cleaned GESIS–DHIS2 mapping. See spatial sources and sectorization schema, lines 54–100; 2018 sectorization and cleaned facility mapping, lines 309–328.
It first repairs geometry and separates Nosy Mitsio from a mainland polygon. It reconciles duplicated FKT codes while preserving the reviewed population totals, validates original codes, and fills missing matches from several rounds of reviewed fuzzy and manual matching. It attaches polygons and uses their topological relationships to identify isolated assignments. Some isolated matches are removed while explicitly protected manual matches remain. See geometry repair and Nosy Mitsio split, lines 56–88; duplicate FKT and population rules, lines 102–121; reviewed matching rounds and geometry joins, lines 123–228; topology checks and isolated-match removal, lines 230–275.
Later passes recover assignments using the 2018 sectorization, apply further manual matches and unmatches, and assign some remaining polygons through a close commune-name match when that commune has one clinic and the assignment does not worsen contiguity. Source: 6_locate_clinics.R. Proposed destination: 24_page-locate-clinics.qmd.
This script assembles candidate coordinates from the cleaned sectorization, MDDSS, WHO and UNICEF master lists, and a separate GPS source, using the clinic-ID crosswalk to connect historical GESIS codes to UIDs. 3.16 Assignment-to-target inventory
This inventory maps the legacy assignments to named responsibilities in the replacement graph. It is a design index; no targets are created or rewired by these tables.
Identifiers use script::variable, for example 1::mapping. The script keys match the filenames in the crosswalk; 999 denotes the utilities and checks denotes data_checks.R. A repeated variable is qualified by its stage because an in-place reassignment can represent a different scientific operation. Function-local values are listed with their owning operation, and short setup/read/normalization steps may share one target. Columns created inside mutate(), summarise(), or := belong to the assigned table; the important column stages are named in the rows rather than proposed as individual targets. Commented-out alternatives are not active assignments; the commented inventory builder in script 2 is retained as provenance for its active inventory read.
Existing means the exact name is declared in the current pipeline notebooks or _targets.R; it does not establish that the target has completed. A row can map to an existing target that already groups several legacy operations. Where the new pipeline changes storage or avoids a large intermediate, the mapping identifies the owning transformation, not an identical R object. Recommended names describe results or responsibilities still to be introduced or separated from a coarse target. Names shared across scripts identify the same producer/consumer handoff, not duplicate proposed targets. Recommended suffixes describe the intended R value or replacement Parquet format; implementation and branching remain to be decided.
Helper definitions are grouped with their owning data responsibilities in the legacy inventory below. In the current notebooks, tar_tangle() also turns top-level function assignments into targets; those use the _fn suffix. Diagnostic and exploratory objects are identified explicitly. Their inclusion preserves the question being asked; it does not promote every scratch expression to a validated scientific rule. The input inventories and current file selectors remain the common staging boundary. Rows for legacy final writes are included even when the write call has no assigned return value. Their replacement handoffs reuse ordinary data targets or name tracked Parquet artifacts.

3.16.1 Target naming convention
Use script-stage_domain_contextual-name_[modification-in-pipeline]_R-data-type, with underscores between words. The modification is optional. The stage identifies the producing legacy script, not the notebook number or the consuming script: s0 through s7, with s4a for measurement cleaning. Exploratory checks use schecks. Shared utility operations keep the stage of their owning transformation. Common staging inputs use s0_pipeline.

title: 4  Render In Isolation
text:
Use scripts/render-isolated from the repository root. It renders a private, data-free staging copy so concurrent jobs do not share Quarto’s mutable cache. Only a successful site and files recorded by quarto-emit are promoted back.






Important Prerequisite: Confirm The Render Boundary



The host needs bash, rsync, mktemp, and quarto. Do not run two publishing renders against the same checkout simultaneously because both would promote to the same docs/ directory.








Tip Procedure: Emit The Isolated Render Wrapper



#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

script_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)
project_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "${script_dir}/.." && pwd)
stage_dir=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/quarto-render.XXXXXXXX")
trap 'rm -rf -- "$stage_dir"' EXIT

export XDG_CACHE_HOME="${stage_dir}/xdg-cache"
export XDG_DATA_HOME="${stage_dir}/xdg-data"
export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="${stage_dir}/xdg-runtime"
mkdir -p "$XDG_CACHE_HOME" "$XDG_DATA_HOME" "$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR"

# The Manual does not consume protected data or mutable runtime state.
rsync -a \
  --exclude '.git' \
  --exclude '.jj' \
  --exclude '.quarto' \
  --exclude '.spack-env' \
  --exclude '.uvr' \
  --exclude '_targets' \
  --exclude 'artifacts' \
  --exclude 'data' \
  --exclude 'docs' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/.quarto' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/_site' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/site_libs' \
  --exclude 'notebooks/*labbook' \
  "$project_dir/" "$stage_dir/project/"

(
  cd "$stage_dir/project"
  quarto render notebooks "$@"
)

emit_manifest="$stage_dir/project/.quarto/quarto-emit-manifest.tsv"
stage_project=$(realpath -e "$stage_dir/project")
if [[ -f "$emit_manifest" ]]; then
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r emitted_path source_page; do
    [[ -n "$emitted_path" && -n "$source_page" ]] || continue
    case "$source_page" in
      "$stage_project"/notebooks/*) ;;
      *) echo "Refusing emit source outside notebooks: $source_page" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    staged_file=$(realpath -e "$(dirname "$source_page")/$emitted_path") || {
      echo "Generated file is missing: $emitted_path" >&2
      exit 1
    }
    case "$staged_file" in
      "$stage_project"/*) ;;
      *) echo "Refusing emit target outside staged project: $staged_file" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
    destination="$project_dir/${staged_file#"$stage_project"/}"
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$destination")"
    rsync -a "$staged_file" "$destination"
  done < "$emit_manifest"
fi

rsync -a --delete "$stage_dir/project/docs/" "$project_dir/docs/"

title: 9  Declare the Native Runtime

title: 10  Customize and Build the Runtime
text:
The Jinja extension adds uvr, Quarto, ARF, and the Spack view to Spack’s generated Singularity recipe. ARF is installed from its pinned, checksummed Linux Rust-binary release. The image supplies R and its native runtime dependencies; uvr retains ownership of project-library and cache resolution at runtime.
The extension configures only image-owned executable, header, metadata, and shared-library search paths. It does not set UVR_LIBRARY, UVR_CACHE_DIR, R_LIBS_USER, or R_LIBS: those paths are project state, so uvr resolves them after the repository is mounted at /work.
ARF dynamically loads R’s C API rather than merely starting an R subprocess. The template therefore preserves the environment emitted by Spack’s parent template, including the R library directory contributed by environment activation. The ARF smoke test starts a headless R session under --cleanenv- equivalent image conditions, which catches a missing libR.so or one of its transitive native libraries.
The container also owns a UTF-8 locale invariant: LANG and LC_ALL are set to C.UTF-8 in the image environment. The runner uses --cleanenv, which otherwise leaves R in the ASCII C locale. In that locale, R’s list.files() turns a valid combining-accent filename byte sequence into literal text such as <cc><81>, creating a path that cannot exist. Setting the invariant in the image makes filename enumeration deterministic and independent of the host login locale. The build-time %test runs before Singularity applies this image environment, so the post-build verification below is the check that the invariant is actually active at runtime.






Important Prerequisite: Confirm The Builder And Container Runtime

test -r artifacts/containers/spack-builder.sif

title: 12  Run the Project Environment
text:
The runner is the only place that selects the image, cleans the host environment, and binds writable project state. Interactive shells, explicit command execution, and Slurm all consume this same boundary.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

project_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)

usage() {
  cat <<'EOF'
Usage:
  mdg-healthshed-clinic-data [shell [SHELL_OPTION...]]
  mdg-healthshed-clinic-data exec COMMAND [ARG...]

With no arguments, open a shell in /work. Commands must use the explicit
`exec` subcommand.
EOF
}

action=${1:-shell}
if (( $# > 0 )); then
  shift
fi

case "${action}" in
  shell) ;;
  exec)
    if (( $# == 0 )); then
      echo "The exec subcommand requires a command." >&2
      usage >&2
      exit 64
    fi
    ;;
  -h|--help)
    usage
    exit 0
    ;;
  *)
    echo "Unknown subcommand: ${action}" >&2
    usage >&2
    exit 64
    ;;
esac

local_env="${project_dir}/containers/runtime/local.env"
if [[ -f "${local_env}" ]]; then
  set -a
  source "${local_env}"
  set +a
fi

runtime=${CONTAINER_RUNTIME:-apptainer}
if ! command -v "${runtime}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  runtime=singularity
fi
command -v "${runtime}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
  echo "Neither apptainer nor singularity is available." >&2
  exit 127
}

image=${MDG_HEALTHSHED_CLINIC_DATA_IMAGE:-"${project_dir}/artifacts/containers/mdg-healthshed-clinic-data.sif"}
test -r "${image}" || {
  echo "Container image not readable: ${image}" >&2
  echo "Build it from the Infrastructure pages or set MDG_HEALTHSHED_CLINIC_DATA_IMAGE." >&2
  exit 1
}

runtime_options=(
  --cleanenv
  --bind "${project_dir}:/work"
  --pwd /work
)

case "${action}" in
  shell)
    exec "${runtime}" shell "${runtime_options[@]}" "$@" "${image}"
    ;;
  exec)
    exec "${runtime}" exec "${runtime_options[@]}" "${image}" "$@"
    ;;
esac

title: 15  Curate the Healthshed Clinic Data
text:
This page declares the Wave 3 preparation targets tangled by _targets.R.






Important Prerequisite: Approve The Curation Contract



The source-inspection page must first record the source schema, record grain, stable keys, pre-/post-DHIS2 boundary, missing-value semantics, validation rules, and disclosure controls.








Tip Procedure: Declare The Parquet Transformation Boundary



Declare the shared file-to-file transformation used by this page and by the clinic-month inventory. Each caller supplies its dependencies and output path.
The helper below opens Parquet inputs with automatic materialization into R disabled, applies the supplied transformation, and writes the result through DuckDB. Only the output path crosses the target boundary. Input paths, output paths, and transformation dependencies stay explicit at each call site.
s0_pipeline_parquet_transform_fn <- function(
  input_paths, output_path, transform, read_options = list()
) {
  input_paths <- unname(as.character(input_paths))
  stopifnot(
    length(input_paths) > 0L,
    all(file.exists(input_paths)),
    length(output_path) == 1L, !is.na(output_path), nzchar(output_path),
    is.function(transform)
  )

  relation <- duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb(
    input_paths,
    prudence = "stingy",
    options = read_options
  )
  result <- transform(relation)

  dir.create(dirname(output_path), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  duckplyr::compute_parquet(result, output_path)
  output_path
}








Tip Procedure: Read One Raw RMA File With Explicit Types



In this first section of the script, we take raw files and prepare them by aggregating them into a tracked Parquet file, one row per clinic-year-month, and one column per health outcome-age-sex.
Applies only to 2020-2022 data.
We’ve also opted-in to using DuckDB via the duckplyr package to avoid in-memory limitations.
library(targets)
library(readr)
library(openxlsx)
library(duckplyr)
library(cli)

tar_load(s0_pipeline_inputs_raw_chr)
We have a variable number of missing values in our first rows of data, so we’ll need to ensure they don’t get read as logical NAs. The duckplyr options list allows us to force DOUBLE and VARCHAR types:
s0_clinic_RMA_read_nonlogical_fn <- function(filepath){

  readr_spec <- spec_csv(filepath) 
  spec_names <- names(readr_spec$cols)

  readr_spec %>%
    as.character() %>%
    str_split_1("") %>%
    tibble(spec = .) %>%
    mutate(
      name = spec_names,
      duckdb_dtype = case_when(
        str_detect(name, regex("description", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "VARCHAR",
        spec == "c" ~ "VARCHAR",
        spec == "d" ~ "DOUBLE",
        spec == "l" ~ "DOUBLE",
        .default = "DOUBLE"
      )
    ) %>%
    select(name, duckdb_dtype) %>%
    deframe() -> duckdb_spec

  
  # Set the CSV dialect explicitly. Auto-detection samples only the first
  # rows, so a quoted comma appearing later can otherwise be misclassified as
  # an extra column.
  read_csv_duckdb(
    filepath,
    options = list(
      types = list(duckdb_spec),
      delim = ",",
      quote = "\"",
      escape = "\""
    )
  ) %>%
    return()
  
}








Tip Procedure: Declare The Clinic-Month Maximum Reduction



Define the reducer shared by the per-file and cross-file aggregation stages. Missing grouping keys fail before a result can be written.
The reductions below use operations that duckplyr translates to DuckDB. DuckDB’s MAX() ignores null values and returns null for an all-null group, which preserves the behavior of the previous max_or_na() helper without materializing columns in R.
s0_clinic_RMA_summarise_group_max_fn <- function(df) {
  grouping_columns <- c("organisationunitid", "periodname")
  missing_grouping_columns <- setdiff(grouping_columns, names(df))
  if (length(missing_grouping_columns)) {
    stop(
      "Cannot calculate clinic-month maxima; missing grouping column(s): ",
      paste(missing_grouping_columns, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  df |>
    summarise(
      across(
        -all_of(grouping_columns),
        ~ max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .by = all_of(grouping_columns)
    )
}








Tip Procedure: Write One Reduced Parquet Branch



Read one source file, remove redundant columns, compute its clinic-month maxima, and write the branch artifact. The small row-count diagnostics are collected for the execution log; the measurement table stays in DuckDB.
s0_clinic_RMA_process_csv_fn <- function(csv_path, output_path=here("data/intermediates"), drop_cols = c("organisationunitcode", "organisationunitdescription")) {
  stopifnot(length(csv_path) == 1L, file.exists(csv_path))
  
  cli_alert_info(paste("Working on:", csv_path))
  
  # Read file with type-safe reader
  temp_df <- s0_clinic_RMA_read_nonlogical_fn(csv_path)
  
  # Drop the extra columns if they exist
  temp_df <- temp_df %>%
    select(-any_of(drop_cols))
  
  # Calculate diagnostics in DuckDB and collect only the two scalar results.
  file_stats <- temp_df |>
    summarise(
      group_rows = n(),
      .by = c(organisationunitid, periodname)
    ) |>
    summarise(
      rows = sum(group_rows),
      duplicate_rows = sum(group_rows - 1L)
    ) |>
    collect()

  cli_alert_info(paste(
    "Successfully created dataframe for", csv_path, "with shape",
    file_stats$rows[[1]], "x", length(names(temp_df))
  ))
  cli_alert_info(paste(
    "Number of duplicate clinic-month-year records:",
    file_stats$duplicate_rows[[1]]
  ))
  
  # Description fields are assigned VARCHAR when the CSV relation is created.
  result = s0_clinic_RMA_summarise_group_max_fn(temp_df)
  
  dir.create(dirname(output_path), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  compute_parquet(result, output_path)

  output_path
}
s0_clinic_RMA_process_csv_fn() intentionally accepts exactly one path, and never holds other input tables in memory. _targets.R selects the RMA_W3_FULL paths and defines a dynamic map() branch for each path outside this notebook. That makes each CSV independently schedulable and means the branch artifacts contain parquet files rather than raw csvs. Dynamic branching enables parallel execution; the approved Slurm allocation and selected targets backend determine how many branches run concurrently.
The second reduction in _targets.R combines the smaller branch summaries and takes the clinic-month maximum again. This is equivalent to taking the maximum over the fully combined raw data because maximum is associative:
[ () = ((), , ()) ]
This two-stage reduction was introduced after the raw-table aggregation was OOM-killed with a 120 GiB Slurm allocation. It is a memory-scaling change, not a change to the numeric maximum rule. The current reducer retains the prior rule for every non-grouping field; a later curation decision should define field-specific behavior for names, descriptions, and codes rather than treating a lexicographic character maximum as scientific metadata.






WarningWhy aggregation stays in DuckDB



The per-file reductions completed, but the final target was OOM-killed in a 120 GiB Slurm allocation. The diagnostic evidence is that files can have zero duplicate clinic-month keys. In that situation, a per-file group maximum has nearly the same cardinality as the input, so the previous R-based final target needed to materialize all branch summaries at once. Increasing the requested memory is not the next proposed experiment.
The per-file target now implements a disk-backed DuckDB/duckplyr boundary. Its stages are:

preserve the existing one-file CSV reading, UTF-8, and type-normalization behavior;
execute each per-file clinic-month MAX reduction in DuckDB;
write each branch result to Parquet without materializing it in R.

The final target below reads all branch Parquet paths as one DuckDB relation, executes the final clinic-month reduction, and persists that result through another file target.
The aim is to preserve the original code’s transformation logic as closely as possible. The change is the execution engine and storage boundary, not a redesign of the data-cleaning rules. Before implementation, the output schema and reducer for metadata fields must be made explicit: numeric measures use maximum, whereas names, descriptions, and codes require a domain-specific rule. DuckDB and duckplyr are declared runtime dependencies.










Tip Procedure: Combine The Reduced Branches



Apply the same reduction to the branch files to obtain one tracked group-maximum artifact. No raw measurement table needs to be collected into R.
Calculate the group maxima across all branch artifacts with the shared helper. union_by_name preserves columns that occur in only some source files.
#| format: file
s0_clinic_RMA_W3_group_max_parquet <- s0_pipeline_parquet_transform_fn(
  input_paths = s0_clinic_RMA_W3_within_file_max_parquet,
  output_path = "data/intermediates/RMA_W3_group_max.parquet",
  transform = s0_clinic_RMA_summarise_group_max_fn,
  read_options = list(union_by_name = TRUE)
)








Tip Procedure: Crosswalk with GESIS Data



Our next step is to crosswalk the clinic data with GESIS DHIS data to get the exact questions for each measure.
#| format: file
s0_gesis_xwalk_raw_csv <- s0_pipeline_inputs_raw_chr |>
  str_subset("mapping DHIS2 GESIS 2010 2022")
s0_gesis_xwalk_nonmissing_uid_df <- read_csv(s0_gesis_xwalk_raw_csv) |>
  select(UID...12, code_fs, TYPE, FS) |>
  rename(organisationunitid = UID...12) |> #correct the naming of organisationunitid
  distinct() |>                            #tidy up missingness
  filter(!is.na(organisationunitid))








Tip Procedure: Write The Cleaned Wave 3 Table



Use the descriptive crosswalk and the reviewed period-specific substitutions to produce the cleaned Parquet artifact.
Lastly, we left_join the RMA wave 3 data with this crosswalk on Organisation. The last bit of cleaning correctly maps diagnoses that changed names slightly between wave 3 subwaves
#| format: file
s0_clinic_RMA_W3_clean_parquet <- s0_pipeline_parquet_transform_fn(
  input_paths = s0_clinic_RMA_W3_group_max_parquet,
  output_path = here("data/intermediates/clinic_RMA_W3_clean.parquet"),
  transform = function(relation) {
    relation |>
      left_join(as_duckdb_tibble(s0_gesis_xwalk_nonmissing_uid_df), by = "organisationunitid") |>
      mutate(
        # rows of AME where periodcode > 202300 should be values of AME prem;
        `T13: AME 0-6 mois` = if_else(
          periodcode > 202300,  `T13: AME premiere heure 0-6 mois`, `T13: AME 0-6 mois`
        ),
        # etc
        `T13: AME 1ère heure` = if_else(
          periodcode > 202300, `T13: AME premiere heure 1ère heure`, `T13: AME 1ère heure`
        ),
        `MIDs pour groupe à risque (migrants/réfugiés/personnes déplacées)` = if_else(
          periodcode > 202300, `CHU CHRR T26 MIDs pour groupe à risque (migrants/réfugiés/personnes déplacées)`, `MIDs pour groupe à risque (migrants/réfugiés/personnes déplacées)`
        )
      ) |>
      # remove redundant
      select(
        -any_of(c(
          "T13: AME premiere heure 0-6 mois",
          "T13: AME premiere heure 1ère heure",
          "CHU CHRR T26 MIDs pour groupe à risque (migrants/réfugiés/personnes déplacées)"
        ))
      ) |>
      mutate(V1 = row_number() - 1L) |>
      select(V1, everything())
  }
)


Important: there is a chance that the assignment of V1 to row number doesn’t work here, due to the fact that the data is now in a Parquet and row numbers are only computed at evaluation time.






Warning Check: Prove Curation Against The Contract



Inspect the completed branches and the persisted summary in an authorized data session. The first expression lists tracked branches. The second collects only an aggregate row count from the completed artifact.

title: 16  Clean the DHIS2–GESIS Mapping
text:
This page translates the reviewed DHIS2–GESIS mapping-cleaning workflow into successive targets. The stage boundaries separate source reads, reviewed corrections, validation queries, and persistence so each decision remains auditable while the execution becomes reproducible.






WarningPreserve reviewed decisions while modernizing



The transformations below preserve the reviewed mapping decisions from the legacy workflow. Each assigned object is a pipeline target. Diagnostic chunks in the final check are deliberately unassigned: they inspect completed targets without adding check-only objects to the graph. The authoring render does not execute them.








Important Prerequisite: Retain The Reviewed Source Evidence



The original mapping CSV and the four manually reviewed workbooks or CSVs must remain available with their provenance intact. Before optimizing a stage, record its input schema, expected row-count change, join cardinality, and the review decision represented by each correction.








Tip Procedure: Load The Mapping Tools



Load the packages used by the mapping transformations and their diagnostic queries. Scientific execution still occurs through the targets graph.

library(targets)

Tip Procedure: Stage 1 — Read And Filter The Source Mapping



This stage reads the base mapping, and assigns names to the four UID levels. It removes the year 2022 and Belalanda from the list.

Tip Procedure: Stage 5 — Reconcile UID-Years With Multiple GESIS Codes



This stage classifies reviewer notes, retains the original internal diagnostic as an executable check, evaluates external GESIS–UID consequences, and applies deletions and renames.

  s0_pipeline_inputs_raw_chr,

  mutate(change = case_when(grepl("the clinic was moved to the district of mandoto", note) ~ "keep", 
                            note %in% c("Same clinic", "OK", "ok") ~ "keep", 
                            grepl("^rename", note) ~ "rename", 
                            grepl("delete|Delete", note) ~ "delete",
                            TRUE ~ as.character(NA)), 
         code_fs = as.character(code_fs)) 
# started with 36 UID-years with multiple GESIS 
# there are 2 deletions, 16 renames, and 18 cases where its just two codes for the same clinic
# --> 18 UID-years with multiple GESIS at the end
# make the change 
s1_gesis_xwalk_multiple_codes_reconciled_df <- s1_gesis_xwalk_uid_filled_df %>%
  # the UIDs got dropped when we rename, which only matters in one case 
  # whe the row needs to be deleted, so separately add in the delete cases vs rest
  left_join(s1_gesis_multiple_codes_reviewed_df %>%
              filter(change == "delete") %>% 
              select(cAnnee, code_fs, fs_uid, change),
            by = c("cAnnee", "code_fs", "fs_uid")) %>%
  filter(change != "delete" | is.na(change)) %>% 
  select(-change) %>% 
  left_join(s1_gesis_multiple_codes_reviewed_df %>%
              filter(change != "delete") %>% 
              select(cAnnee, code_fs, change,
                     fs_uid_correct = UID,

            by = c("cAnnee", "code_fs")) %>%
  mutate(fs_uid = case_when(change == "rename" & fs_uid_correct == "No UID" ~ "",
                            change == "rename" ~ fs_uid_correct,
                            TRUE ~ fs_uid),
         FS = case_when(change == "rename" & fs_name_correct != "" ~ fs_name_correct, 
                        TRUE ~ FS)) %>%
  select(-(change:fs_name_correct)) %>%

Tip Procedure: Declare Archive And Text Helpers



Resolve exact archive-member suffixes and extract only the selected input into a temporary directory. Each reader must return a materialized small object before extraction cleanup; no temporary path becomes a downstream input.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(duckplyr)
library(targets)

s3_dictionary_archive_member_fn <- function(archive, suffix) {
  members <- utils::unzip(archive, list = TRUE)$Name
  hits <- members[endsWith(members, paste0("/", suffix)) &
                    !grepl("(^|/)__MACOSX/", members)]
  if (length(hits) != 1L) stop("Expected one archive member for: ", suffix)
  unname(hits)
}
s3_dictionary_archive_read_fn <- function(archive, member, reader) {
  stopifnot(length(member) == 1L, !grepl("^/|(^|/)\\.\\.(/|$)", member))
  extraction_dir <- tempfile("dictionary-input-")
  dir.create(extraction_dir)
  on.exit(unlink(extraction_dir, recursive = TRUE), add = TRUE)
  path <- utils::unzip(archive, files = member, exdir = extraction_dir)
  stopifnot(length(path) == 1L, file.exists(path))
  reader(path)
}

s3_dictionary_read_csv_fn <- function(archive, member) {
  s3_dictionary_archive_read_fn(archive, member, function(path) {
    read.csv(path, fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  })
}
Apply the legacy wording substitutions sequentially. Unequal non-scalar pattern/replacement vectors fail explicitly instead of calling the legacy undefined error() function.
s3_diagnosis_multiple_gsub_fn <- function(patterns, replacements, x) {
  if (length(patterns) != length(replacements) &&
      length(patterns) != 1L && length(replacements) != 1L) {
    stop("Pattern and replacement must have equal length or be scalar.")
  }
  count <- max(length(patterns), length(replacements))
  patterns <- rep_len(patterns, count)
  replacements <- rep_len(replacements, count)
  for (i in seq_len(count)) x <- gsub(patterns[[i]], replacements[[i]], x)
  x
}

Select local column names with all_of()/pick() when the helper runs. This preserves grouped column lookup while avoiding premature unquotation when tar_tangle() declares the function target.
s3_diagnosis_aggregate_to_wave_fn <- function(df, target_wave,
                                     all_waves = paste0("wave", c(1:2, "3A", "3B"))) {
  other_waves = setdiff(all_waves, target_wave)
  target_col = paste0(target_wave, "_colname")
  target_desc = paste0(target_wave, "_description")
  other_col = paste0(other_waves, "_colname")
  filter(df, if_any(all_of(target_col), ~ !is.na(.x))) %>%
    summarise(description = unique(pick(all_of(target_desc))[[1L]]),
              across(all_of(other_col),
                     ~if(any(is.na(.x))){NA}else{paste(unique(.x), collapse = " + ")}),
              .by = all_of(target_col)) %>%
    mutate(wave1_colname = ifelse(n() == 1, wave1_colname, NA),
           .by = c(wave1_colname)) %>%
    mutate(wave2_colname = ifelse(n() == 1, wave2_colname, NA),
           .by = c(wave2_colname)) %>%
    mutate(wave3A_colname = ifelse(n() == 1, wave3A_colname, NA),
           .by = c(wave3A_colname)) %>%
    mutate(wave3B_colname = ifelse(n() == 1, wave3B_colname, NA),
           .by = c(wave3B_colname)) %>%
    return
}

Validate the source-expression contract without evaluating expressions as R code. Report reused complete expressions, repeated summands, and terms absent from the corresponding source schema. Missing expressions remain allowed; they indicate that a comparable definition is unavailable in that wave.
s3_diagnosis_validate_fn <- function(dictionary, wave3_schema, wave12_dictionary) {
  empty <- tibble(var = character(), wave = character(), issue = character(),
                  expression = character())
  issues <- list(empty)
  for (wave in c("wave1", "wave2", "wave3A", "wave3B")) {
    expressions <- dictionary[[paste0(wave, "_colname")]]
    columns <- if (wave %in% c("wave1", "wave2")) {
      wave12_dictionary$Column.Name
    } else wave3_schema$w3_colname
    reused <- duplicated(expressions) | duplicated(expressions, fromLast = TRUE)
    for (i in which(!is.na(expressions))) {
      terms <- strsplit(expressions[[i]], " + ", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
      problems <- c(if (reused[[i]]) "reused_expression",
                    if (anyDuplicated(terms)) "repeated_summand",
                    if (any(!terms %in% columns)) "unknown_source_column")
      if (length(problems)) issues[[length(issues) + 1L]] <- tibble(
        var = dictionary$var[[i]], wave = wave,
        issue = problems, expression = expressions[[i]]
      )
    }
  }
  bind_rows(issues)
}

The graph inventories staged paths and dynamically branches the approved W3 CSV preparation and legacy clinic-month inventory work. Branching is declared here rather than in the transformation notebooks: each notebook defines one-file transformation logic, while this graph defines dependencies and the scheduler can distribute independent branches. Clinic-month branches track one Parquet file per monthly member of the staged ZIP. Page 20 combines their paths into a single Parquet inventory before collecting the reduced identity table. Page 21 constructs the cross-wave diagnosis dictionary from the prepared Wave 3 schema and archived source dictionaries and translations.






NoteTrack Data At Each Target Boundary



The current graph executes each per-file maximum in DuckDB and writes the result to a branch-specific Parquet file. targets stores those file paths rather than attempting to serialize live duckplyr relations. Page 18 declares the final cross-file aggregation and cleaned Parquet output, included through tar_tangle(). In-memory tables remain ordinary data targets; source files and derived Parquet paths use format = "file" so their contents are tracked.
